title: Three ways to replicate stock with options, and the one that can blow up
summary: You can replicate stock with a 95 delta call, an at-the-money synthetic (long call, short put), or a ZEBRA. The synthetic can blow up an account because the short put grows without limit as the stock falls. The 95 delta call is simplest and costs a fraction of the shares. Its small extrinsic value is mostly offset by interest on the saved cash, but it pays no dividend.

steps.caption: The stock trades at $100. Both positions behave like 100 shares near the current price.
The 95 delta call: one line item, a fraction of the share cost, and the loss stops at the premium.
The at-the-money synthetic: long call plus short put. Below $100 the short put loses more and more.
In a big drop the synthetic keeps losing while the call's loss is capped. This is the blow-up risk.
The call's extrinsic value is a small cost. Interest on the saved cash usually offsets most of it.

takeaways: A 95 delta call is the simplest stock replacement with a known maximum loss.
An at-the-money synthetic has a short put with stock-like downside and margin risk.
The cash saved stays as dry powder and earns interest.
Calls pay no dividends, and you can sell calls against the core to make a poor man's covered call.
caveats: The ZEBRA is mentioned but not explained in the transcript, so it is not modeled.
Interest offsetting the extrinsic value depends on rates and volatility at the time.

backtest.note: 95 delta call about six months out as stock replacement, rolled with 60 days left.
